name: Sleep, arousal and EEG basics
summary: Wakefulness is maintained by the ascending arousal system of the brainstem and hypothalamus, cholinergic, monoaminergic and orexinergic, which drives the thalamus and cortex, and sleep is imposed by the preoptic hypothalamus, which switches those systems off, with the REM state generated in the pons. The electroencephalogram records the summed synaptic currents of cortical pyramidal cells, paced by thalamocortical loops, and its rhythms map these states: alpha in relaxed wakefulness, theta and spindles in light sleep, delta in deep sleep, low-voltage fast activity with eye movements and atonia in REM. Disorders of this machinery, narcolepsy, REM behavior disorder, insomnia after hypothalamic lesions, coma from brainstem damage and the encephalopathies that slow the EEG, are read directly from the physiology.

sections.heading: The ascending arousal system
sections.body: Cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei activate the thalamus, and monoaminergic neurons of the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), the raphe (serotonin), the tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine) and the ventral tegmental area (dopamine) together with the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons activate the cortex directly; the orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus stabilize the whole system in the waking state. Damage to the paramedian upper pons and midbrain, where these pathways converge, produces coma, and bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction produces hypersomnolence, whereas hemispheric lesions cause coma only when they compress the brainstem. Loss of the orexin neurons produces narcolepsy, in which the wake state collapses into sleep and REM intrudes into waking as cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

sections.heading: The sleep switch and the sleep cycle
sections.body: The ventrolateral and median preoptic nuclei inhibit every arousal nucleus with GABA and galanin at sleep onset and are inhibited by them during waking, a mutually inhibitory flip-flop that gives sharp transitions and is biased by the homeostatic pressure of adenosine (blocked by caffeine) and the circadian signal from the suprachiasmatic nucleus through the dorsomedial hypothalamus. Non-REM sleep deepens through stages N1 to N3 as thalamic neurons hyperpolarize and generate spindles and then delta waves; REM sleep is generated by the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the pons, which produces cortical activation, rapid eye movements and, through the medullary reticular formation, the atonia of skeletal muscle. Cycles of 90 minutes repeat four to six times, with REM lengthening toward morning. Loss of REM atonia produces dream enactment, the REM sleep behavior disorder that precedes synucleinopathies by years.

sections.heading: Reading the EEG
sections.body: Scalp electrodes record 10 to 100 microvolt fluctuations produced by synchronous postsynaptic potentials in the apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells; the rhythms depend on thalamocortical pacing and cortical health. Normal waking shows a posterior alpha rhythm of 8 to 13 Hz that attenuates with eye opening, drowsiness shows theta, N2 sleep shows sleep spindles and K-complexes, and N3 shows high-amplitude delta; REM shows low-voltage fast activity with sawtooth waves. Diffuse slowing indicates encephalopathy of any cause, triphasic waves suggest metabolic or hepatic encephalopathy, focal slowing indicates a structural lesion, periodic lateralized discharges indicate an acute cortical injury such as herpes encephalitis or stroke, generalized periodic complexes in a demented patient suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and burst suppression or electrocerebral silence indicate deep anesthesia or catastrophic injury. Epileptiform spikes and sharp waves are the subject of the epilepsy entry.

sections.heading: Clinical disorders of sleep and arousal
sections.body: Narcolepsy type 1 is orexin deficiency with cataplexy and low CSF hypocretin; idiopathic hypersomnia and sleep apnea are the other causes of daytime sleepiness, and the multiple sleep latency test with a preceding polysomnogram separates them. REM sleep behavior disorder is a pontine sign and predicts Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia or multiple system atrophy. Insomnia follows preoptic and anterior hypothalamic lesions; circadian disorders follow suprachiasmatic damage and blindness. Coma reflects damage to the arousal system or bilateral hemispheric dysfunction, and its grading, the brainstem reflexes and the EEG pattern determine prognosis; the persistent vegetative state retains sleep-wake cycles without awareness, and the locked-in state retains both. Sedative and antihistamine drugs act on these same nuclei, which is why they cause both sleep and delirium.

keyPoints: Coma needs a lesion of the paramedian upper brainstem or of both hemispheres; a single hemisphere cannot produce it without herniation
Narcolepsy is orexin loss: sleep attacks, cataplexy and REM intrusions
REM sleep behavior disorder is a pontine sign that predicts synuclein disease years before parkinsonism
The posterior alpha rhythm that blocks with eye opening is the first thing to find on a normal EEG
Triphasic waves, periodic lateralized discharges and burst suppression each tell a different story: metabolic, focal cortical injury, catastrophic
pearls: Ask about dream enactment in every patient with parkinsonism or dementia: the answer dates the disease
A slow EEG says encephalopathy, not which one; the history and the metabolic screen say which
Sedatives and antihistamines act on the same nuclei that produce delirium in the elderly
pitfalls: Daytime sleepiness in a snorer is sleep apnea until a sleep study says otherwise; do not label it narcolepsy

imaging.normalAppearance: Sleep disorders are diagnosed by polysomnography and the multiple sleep latency test; MRI is reserved for secondary causes (hypothalamic, pontine and thalamic lesions) and coma.

pathology.pathology: Paramedian thalamic and midbrain infarct with hypersomnolence
pathology.finding: Bilateral paramedian thalamic restricted diffusion with or without a midbrain lesion (artery of Percheron).

pathology.pathology: Pontine tegmental lesion with REM disturbance
pathology.finding: Lesion of the dorsolateral pontine tegmentum (infarct, demyelination, tumor) in a patient with new dream enactment or cataplexy.

pathology.pathology: Hypothalamic lesion with narcolepsy or insomnia
pathology.finding: Mass, inflammation or infarct of the lateral or anterior hypothalamus with secondary narcolepsy or loss of sleep.
